newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rybkin ends first day at work with plea for calm.
newsitem.headline: Rybkin ends first day at work with plea for calm.

text.p: New Russian security chief Ivan Rybkin has spent his first full day at work trying to undo some of the damage done during his tempestuous predecessor's term while making clear he has no intention of being a lightweight.

Rybkin, a moderate former parliamentary speaker, called for a stop to the kind of public rows between Kremlin officials which became the norm during Alexander Lebed's explosive four months in office which ended in his sacking on Thursday.
"Policies should be open and transparent for all to see," Rybkin told Ekho Moskvy radio on Sunday.
"But it is impermissible that there should be public fights between leading officials -- they should deal with their problems by the book," said Rybkin, who turned 50 on Sunday.
President Boris Yeltsin appointed Rybkin to Lebed's old posts of secretary to the powerful Security Council as well as his personal envoy to Chechnya on Saturday.

Rybkin has none of Lebed's bluntness but just in case anyone might think the new man would easily be pushed aside, he suggested that the work of the three "power ministries" should be much more closely coordinated.

Rybkin said the interior, defence and security ministers should only report to Yeltsin when a coordinator was present and that a new body should be set up to control all the weapons and equipment used by the three ministries' forces.
"It's difficult. I understand the full weight of the problem on my shoulders...I am sure we'll find a close partnership for the good of Russia," he told Russian television.
But it seemed highly unlikely that the three ministries, who jealously guard the right to operate their own armed forces, would agree to give up control of their weapons.
The idea could also provide more ammunition for Lebed, who described Rybkin as a failed bureaucrat who had no idea as to how Russia's security could be ensured.
But his successor declined to exchange taunts and was at pains to praise Lebed for the peace deal which ended the 21-month Chechen war on August 31.

"The days have gone when we used to tease each other because someone's nose was too big or their ears were the wrong shape. We understood this was wrong when still at school -- it's totally useless," Rybkin said.
He won cautious approval from the Chechen separatists, who had previously seen Lebed as the only hope for a permanent end to the bitter war in which tens of thousands have died.

"I want to assure (the Chechen leadership) that the talks will continue. We have no intention of stepping back from agreements which have already been signed. We want peaceful solutions to all aspects of this problem," he said.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has also said the peace deal will not be scrapped and promised the Security Council would continue to deal with the affair, a clear hint that hardline ministers will not be allowed to wreck the treaty.
Rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov, speaking to reporters in the capital Grozny, welcomed the Kremlin's approach.

"As far as this can influence events, it's hard to say 100 percent, but in general the statements of Chernomyrdin and Rybkin that the Security Council will be pre-eminent in this question give us hope. We'll see," he said.
